source: Araya (2025) Do chains-of-thought of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: Three reasoning LLMs (Gemini, ChatGPT, DeepSeek) solved one Bayesian puzzle in zero-shot with probability algebra only. None used natural frequencies unprompted. When told to use Gigerenzer's natural-frequency strategy, they used it only partly or wrongly. The author calls this a bias for symbolic probability language.
numbers: 3 models, 1 problem family, 4 prompt stages (plain; +natural frequencies; +blocks; +colour). No accuracy rates reported. Example: ChatGPT with the natural-frequency prompt still reached a wrong 50% answer.
quote: None of the three LLMs used ecologically valid formats.
limits: Qualitative. Tiny sample. Not a test of whether counts raise accuracy; it shows that the format is not adopted by default. Closes gap 7 only in part.
agent_relevance: Do not assume that writing 'use natural frequencies' changes the model's arithmetic. Make code build the counts table and give the model the counts, not the instruction.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts (UoT), full text with Table 2 equal-token comparison
finding: At matched GPT-4 token budgets, UoT (information-gain style reward over a possibility set) beats a Tree-of-Thought baseline that is told to ask questions that halve the search space. The gap is large on 20 Questions but small on the medical set.
numbers: Table 2 (GPT-4, closed set, success %): 4.5k tokens: Adapted-ToT D=3 20Q 33.8, medical (MD) 85.1, troubleshooting (TB) 60.3; Pruned UoT 4.7k tokens 48.1, 88.4, 63.2. 9k tokens: Adapted-ToT D=4 40.9, 86.7, 63.7; UoT D=3 54.4, 92.5, 66.0. So on MD the gain over the halving heuristic is +3.3 points at about 4.6k tokens and +5.8 at about 9k. Original-ToT MD 65.3; CoT-SC (k=33) MD 37.6. DX 97.0 with GPT-4 closed set; the abstract's 38.1% average is versus direct prompting.
limits: Medical task is simplified (DX: 104 dialogues, 5 diseases; MedDG 15 diseases). Closed set means the answer options are given. Outcomes are simulated by an LLM patient, not calibrated. The 38.1% headline is against direct prompting, not against the halving heuristic.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: the halving heuristic captures most of the gain on medical diagnosis (85.1 vs 88.4 at equal tokens). Expected-information-gain adds a few points, not tens. Start with 'most discriminating question' and add EIG only if measured to help.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026, ICLR) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs, full text
finding: Selecting questions by true expected information gain (with a noisy-answer likelihood) beats both direct prompting and a Split baseline that picks the question that most evenly splits the hypotheses. Entropy-only selection (a deterministic-answer shortcut) gives smaller gains.
numbers: 20 Questions, 100 targets per set, success % at turn 20 (Prompt-Only / Split / CoT / BED-LLM / Entropy): Animals GPT-4o 45/83/62/93/88; Animals Mistral-Large 33/85/35/95/83; Celebrities GPT-4o 45/63/63/86/64; Celebrities Mistral-Large 19/63/42/91/68; Things GPT-4o 34/40/49/64/49; Things Llama-3.3-70B 34/46/35/55/48. BED-LLM gain over Split ranges about +2 to +28 points, largest on Celebrities. Abstract: +37.4 points over direct prompting on average. The Entropy ablation gave no gain over Prompt-Only in preference elicitation.
quote: we advise against making deterministic likelihood assumptions
limits: Not medical. 20 Questions and preference elicitation only. 2024-class models (GPT-4o, Llama 3.x, Qwen 2.5). The answer likelihood comes from the same LLM, so it is not calibrated against real patients. A mismatched answerer (Qwen vs GPT-4o-mini) kept the gains. Token cost per question is higher than Split. Author-chosen baselines.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 5 in part: a best-split heuristic (Split) is already a strong baseline (+30 to +40 over prompting); full EIG adds more when answers are noisy. Use the answer-noise term (conditional entropy) in S7, not entropy alone. Medical transfer is untested.

source: Nori et al. (2025) Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models (MAI-DxO), full arXiv text
finding: The orchestrator has roles (hypothesis tracker, test-chooser, challenger, stewardship, checklist) and commits to a diagnosis only when certainty passes a threshold. The paper gives variants but no ablation of the test-chooser role alone.
numbers: SDBench 304 NEJM cases; test set 56. Off-the-shelf o3: 78.6% at $7,850. MAI-DxO (o3, no budget) 81.9% at $4,735. Budgeted variant 79.9% at $2,396. Ensemble 85.5% at $7,184. 21 physicians: 19.9% accuracy, $2,963, 6.6 questions and 7.2 tests per case (764 diagnoses). Single-turn vs batched (test set, o3): both 83.9%; cost $3,991 vs $5,084. Model inference about $0.15 per case.
quote: the baseline seemed to lack a theory of information value
limits: No ablation of any single role. Debate, hypothesis tracking, cost tracking and test choice are bundled. Physicians were barred from search and from LLMs. Hard NEJM cases. Developed on GPT-4.1. Text says $2,396; earlier notes say $2,397.
agent_relevance: Confirms K15 is single-source and confounded. The stop rule is 'certainty over a threshold', stated but not tuned or compared. Gap 9 stays open. The measured part is the cost cut (7,850 to 4,735) at equal or higher accuracy.

source: Nori et al. (2026) Sequential diagnosis with language models, Science (published version)
finding: Published version reports a second dataset and different physician numbers than the preprint.
numbers: 83.2% on NEJM clinicopathological cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED admissions, versus generalist physicians 36.1% and 46.8%.
limits: Only the abstract was read (Europe PMC record). Physician baseline differs from the preprint (19.9%). Component ablations not seen.
agent_relevance: Update K15: the scaffold gain is now peer reviewed, but its parts are still not separated. Use preprint numbers for cost, Science numbers for accuracy.

source: Sci Rep (2026) Large language models generate diagnostic likelihood ratios with low mean bias but wide dispersion
finding: Three OpenAI models were asked, few-shot, for numeric likelihood ratios (LRs) and compared with 700 literature LRs from TheNNT.com. Average bias is nil but single values can be several-fold off. Outputs shrink toward 1.
numbers: 700 LRs, 30 conditions; types: signs/symptoms 59%, history 19%, test results 16%. Literature LRs: median 1, IQR 0.7-2.2, range 0.01-145.9; 56.5% in 0.5-2. Mean bias: GPT-4o 1.02x, o3 0.99x, GPT-5 0.99x. 95% limits of agreement: GPT-5 0.26x-3.70x, o3 0.23x-4.28x, GPT-4o 0.23x-4.53x. Calibration slope: GPT-4o 0.73, o3 0.76, GPT-5 0.88 (R2 0.65, 0.64, 0.68). GPT-5 strength-category kappa 0.78. Lab-test LRs agreed less than history, sign or imaging LRs. Example in paper: pretest 0.50 with LR 1.0 stays 0.50, with LR 4.0 becomes 0.80.
limits: Agreement may be memorisation of TheNNT or its sources (internet off, training exposure not excluded). They did not validate combined posteriors, did not test conditional dependence, and did not compare an LR workflow with an end-to-end LLM answer. OpenAI models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: gives the measured quality of model-elicited LRs (a few-fold error per finding) but not the head-to-head. Gap 2/3: states the chaining test as future work. Carry LR ranges (about 0.3x to 3.7x) not points when the model supplies them; prefer table LRs for lab tests.

source: Feng et al. (2025, ICLR) BIRD: a trustworthy Bayesian inference framework for LLMs
finding: LLM proposes factors and coarse support labels; a Bayesian network fitted to human preference computes the probability. This beats verbalised LLM probabilities and is comparable to chain-of-thought for decisions. It is the closest published head-to-head to 'LLM elicits, code computes'.
numbers: Probability alignment with human judgment: F1 59% for BIRD (two base models), more than 30% above GPT-4 verbalised; still +5% over GPT-4 even in the setting that favours the LLM (pairwise 'EC'). Decision tasks: beats CoT with self-consistency using Llama-3.1 on all benchmarks, about equal with Llama-2; abductive factor sampling +4.4% / +3.9% accuracy over direct factor generation. Abstract: probabilities 30% better than direct LLM baselines.
limits: Not medical. Llama-2, Llama-3.1 and GPT-4 era. Cases where BIRD said 'unknown' were removed for the CoT comparison. Tokens not equalised. Not a 2025-26 frontier model.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open for diagnosis and frontier models, but there is supporting evidence that splitting factor elicitation from the arithmetic helps. Our test (code posterior vs one-shot at equal tokens) is still worth running.

source: Lijmer et al. (1999) Empirical evidence of design-related bias in studies of diagnostic tests, JAMA
finding: Across 184 studies of 218 tests, accuracy is overestimated when the design is weak. The biggest bias comes from enrolling sick people plus a separate healthy control group.
numbers: Relative diagnostic odds ratio (RDOR): diseased-plus-separate-control design 3.0 (95% CI 2.0-4.5); different reference tests for positives and negatives 2.2 (1.5-3.3); no test criteria described 1.7 (1.1-2.5); no population description 1.4 (1.1-1.7); reference read with knowledge of test 1.3 (1.0-1.9). Only 15 of 218 (6.8%) met all 8 criteria; 64 (30%) met at least 6.
limits: Abstract read (Europe PMC record). Effects are on the diagnostic odds ratio, not on LR+ and LR- separately. 1996-97 literature searches.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 numbers: a published DOR can be inflated about 3x by case-control design. A table LR from such a study should carry a range and a design flag, and the agent should discount LRs from weak designs.

source: Leeflang et al. (2013) Variation of a test's sensitivity and specificity with disease prevalence, CMAJ
finding: In 23 meta-analyses, sensitivity or specificity moved with disease prevalence, consistent with patient-spectrum differences and not a fixed property of the test.
numbers: 23 meta-analyses, 416 studies, 10 to 39 per review; median prevalence per review 1% to 77%. From lowest to highest prevalence, sensitivity or specificity changed by 0 to 40 percentage points within a review. Significant (p<0.05) for sensitivity or specificity in 8 of 23 (35%). Specificity tended to be lower at higher prevalence; no systematic effect on sensitivity.
limits: Abstract read. Prevalence is a proxy for spectrum and setting; the causal route is not proven. Effect on LRs is not computed in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a stored LR is not portable across settings. Prefer setting-matched LRs and carry a sensitivity range. A 40-point shift in specificity changes LR+ several-fold.

source: Mulherin and Miller (2002) Spectrum bias or spectrum effect? Subgroup variation in diagnostic test evaluation, Ann Intern Med
finding: The paper argues for the term spectrum effect: subgroup variation is not bias if you stratify. It proposes stratified sensitivity, specificity and LRs.
numbers: No pooled numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Conceptual.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: stratify LRs by presentation (symptom duration, referral setting) in the knowledge table instead of averaging.

source: Preprint (2026) How can spectrum bias impact expectations of test performance: swab-based TB tests modelling
finding: Using one pooled sensitivity overstated real-world performance compared with a model stratified by bacterial load.
numbers: Pooled positive agreement MiniDock 84.8% (95% CI 67.1-93.8), Xpert 93.1% (90.3-95.2). By grade: Very Low / Trace MiniDock 56.5% / 33.8%; Xpert 66.7% / 23.1%. On 1,248 positives (1,033 facility, 215 community) the single-value model predicted 10.8% (MiniDock) and 19.1% (Xpert) more positive results in community settings. Missed 241 vs 228 of 1,248 under the stratified model.
limits: Preprint, abstract only; tuberculosis; agreement with another test, not a gold standard.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a worked case where keeping a range by spectrum stratum changes the expected yield by 10 to 19%, enough to change a decision near a threshold.

source: Commentary (2026) Epidemiological spectrum bias limits the clinical validity of LLM-based rare disease diagnostics
finding: Benchmarks for rare-disease LLM diagnosis use enriched case sets. Monte Carlo runs show positive predictive value collapses at realistic low prevalence.
numbers: No specific figures in the abstract.
limits: Preprint, abstract only, commentary.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, LLM angle: benchmark accuracy of LLM diagnosers is itself inflated by case selection. Re-weight benchmarks to realistic prevalence before tuning thresholds.

source: Johnson et al. (2017) Understanding the effects of conditional dependence in studies of imperfect diagnostic tests, Stat Med
finding: Conditional covariance between two tests equals the product of the shifts in test sensitivities (or specificities) across a hidden subgroup. Simulations found the bias from ignoring it is generally small for moderate covariate effects.
numbers: Maximum covariance arises from a strong dichotomous covariate that shifts both tests. Covariate forms tested: normal, uniform, dichotomous, trichotomous. Illustrated on childhood TB data.
limits: About estimating prevalence and accuracy by latent class models, not clinical posterior chaining. The 'small bias' result may not carry to a chained posterior.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: dependence is strongest when both tests share a hidden driver. Group tests that share a mechanism and take one LR for the group.

source: Dendukuri and Joseph (2001) Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests, Biometrics
finding: With fewer than four tests the dependence cannot be identified from data; the posterior leans on the prior about the correlation.
numbers: Needs at least 4 tests for an identifiable classical solution; the two-test case needs a strong prior on the correlation. Example: Strongyloides in Cambodian refugees.
limits: Abstract only. Estimation setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: pairwise dependence cannot be learned from the usual small data. The agent should widen the posterior interval after chaining, not try to fit correlations.

source: Computed here (2026-11-01): numeric illustration of the independence error when two positive tests are chained
finding: Two tests, each sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.9, prior 0.10, both positive. Multiplying LRs assumes independence and gives 0.90. If false positives are correlated, the true posterior is much lower.
numbers: Independent: 0.900. Joint covariance 0.03 added in both groups: 0.700. 0.05 in both: 0.614. Covariance 0.05 only among the non-diseased: 0.600. 0.08 among the non-diseased: 0.500. Upper limit (the second test a copy of the first): 0.500, the second test adds nothing.
limits: Hand-built toy, not a measured study. Covariance values are assumptions. A calculation, not literature evidence.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the error is bounded, since a copy adds nothing. A safe rule in code: for tests that share a mechanism, cap the combined LR near the larger single LR. Test this on the agent.

source: Williams et al. (2024) Evaluating the use of LLMs to provide clinical recommendations in the Emergency Department, Nat Commun
finding: On real ED visits, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4-turbo recommended radiology, antibiotics and admission for most patients: high sensitivity, very low specificity. Telling the model to 'only suggest if absolutely required' helped little.
numbers: Balanced samples of 10,000 per task. GPT-3.5-turbo radiology: Prompt A sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.13; B 0.96 / 0.22; C 0.96 / 0.23; D (step by step) 0.96 / 0.20. Admission A 1.00 / 0.07, D 0.92 / 0.37. Antibiotics A 0.96 / 0.21, D 0.91 / 0.32. GPT-4-turbo had markedly better specificity for radiology and antibiotics at the cost of sensitivity. Accuracy below a resident by 8% (GPT-4-turbo) and 24% (GPT-3.5) on average.
limits: 2023-24 models; no costs stated in the prompt; ground truth is what clinicians did, not what was needed. Balanced samples exaggerate false-positive share versus real prevalence.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: first measured over-ordering for LLMs. A prompt reminder to be restrictive barely worked, so a gate in code (threshold from stated costs) is more reliable. Not a test of the Pauker-Kassirer rule itself.

source: Qiu et al. (2025) Quantifying the reasoning abilities of LLMs on real-world clinical cases (MedR-Bench), full text
finding: On 1,453 cases, reasoning LLMs recommended examinations with low precision and middling recall. Free turns did not improve recall and led to repeated-request loops.
numbers: Exam recommendation (all diseases, 1-turn) precision / recall: o3-mini 33.75 / 38.47; Gemini-2.0-FT 22.77 / 43.12; DeepSeek-R1 31.50 / 43.61; Qwen-QwQ 24.43 / 39.90; Baichuan-M1 41.78 / 37.88. Free-turn recall: o3-mini 38.22, R1 40.67. Diagnostic accuracy R1: 71.79% 1-turn, 76.18% free-turn, 89.76% with all results given; o3-mini 64.99 to 67.19 (1-turn to free-turn).
limits: Precision is against the exam list real clinicians used, so 'not on the list' is not 'cannot change the action'. Late-2024/early-2025 models.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 9: at best about 42% of requested tests match the real workup. More turns lifted accuracy 2 to 5 points without better test choice. Add a stop or loop guard.

source: Pauker and Kassirer (1980) The threshold approach to clinical decision making, NEJM; formulas re-derived here
finding: Two thresholds: withhold treatment below the testing threshold, treat without testing above the test-treatment threshold, test in between. They depend on test sensitivity, specificity, test risk, and treatment benefit and harm.
numbers: Re-derived from expected utility (B net benefit of treating the diseased, C net harm of treating the non-diseased, Rt test risk): testing threshold L = ((1-Sp)C + Rt) / ((1-Sp)C + Se B); test-treatment threshold U = (Sp C - Rt) / (Sp C + (1-Se) B). Example Se=Sp=0.9, B=C=1, Rt=0: L=0.10, U=0.90; with Rt=0.05: L=0.15, U=0.85. Treatment threshold without testing: C/(B+C)=0.5.
limits: Abstract read (no numbers there). Formulas derived in this session and checked on the symmetric case; not copied from the paper text. One binary test, one treatment, risk-neutral utility.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: the agent can compute L and U in code from stated B, C and test properties. No study was found on whether LLMs obey it.

source: Diagnosis (2026) Balancing benefit, harm, and uncertainty in diagnosis: determining the testing threshold in clinical practice
finding: A framework says testing thresholds are dynamic: they depend on symptom amplitude, time course, patient values, system costs, and test quality and cost.
numbers: No numeric thresholds in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Narrative review.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and K04: thresholds should be inputs from the situation (stated costs), not constants. Still no quantitative values.

source: Diagnosis (2026) Accuracy of emergency physicians' probability estimates for acute coronary syndrome
finding: A staged vignette study replicates the overestimation of pretest probability. Estimates fell as information arrived but stayed above reference.
numbers: 707 respondents, 357 complete (Skane, Sweden). First frame (history and symptoms): median estimate about 70% versus reference range 3-16%. Over-estimation in all frames.
limits: One vignette from one real chest-pain patient; clinicians from one region. Independent of the Morgan dataset. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: K02: a second, independent human source for overestimated pretest probability. Supports base-rate tables over recalled intuition.

source: Hoffrage, Krauss, Martignon, Gigerenzer (2015) Natural frequencies improve Bayesian reasoning in simple and complex inference tasks, Front Psychol (PMC text, first 100,000 characters)
finding: Medical students did far better with natural frequencies than probabilities, and a short frequency-tree training lifted performance more than a Bayes-rule lesson. The paper quotes the 1998 physician result.
numbers: Study 1 (N=64 advanced medical students, Berlin): Task 1 probability 1% vs natural frequency 59%; mean over 4 tasks 7% vs 45%. Study 2 (N=78): Bayes-rule instruction with probabilities 18% and 22% (N=27); frequency-translation instruction with probabilities 40% (N=25); frequency-tree with natural frequencies 73% and 81% (N=26). Quoted: physicians 16 of 24 correct with frequencies vs 1 of 24 with conditional probabilities (Hoffrage and Gigerenzer 1998). The 46% vs 16% of Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 1995 is not in this text, which says only 'almost half'.
limits: Secondary source for the 1995 and 1998 numbers. Eddy 1982, Fagan 1975 and the 1995 paper were not obtainable in this run. Last 26,000 characters not read. Student samples.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 (partial): the frequency effect is replicated in size. For K05 treat 'physicians 1/24 vs 16/24' as quoted, not verified at source.

source: AAN 2026 abstract: Gemini 2.5 Pro vs ChatGPT-5 on neurology vignettes
finding: Two 2025 models have equal diagnostic accuracy, but stated confidence tracks correctness in one and not in the other.
numbers: 51 vignettes (accuracy reported over 50). ChatGPT-5 45/50 (90.0%, CI 78.6-95.7); Gemini 2.5 Pro 44/50 (88.0%, CI 76.2-94.4); McNemar p=0.739. Confidence 0-10: ChatGPT-5 9.42 correct vs 7.80 incorrect (p=0.04); Gemini 9.66 vs 9.67 (not significant). High-confidence critical errors in both.
limits: Conference abstract. Diagnosis confidence, not pretest probability. No ECE or Brier. One specialty.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 (indirect): no study of current models on the Morgan vignettes was found; this says verbalised confidence from 2025 models may carry little signal. Do not gate on stated confidence alone.

source: Behav Res Methods (2026) An LLM canary in the online data coalmine: Bayesian reasoning problems as a capability-gap test
finding: Online participants scored about three times the human ceiling on positive-predictive-value problems, read by the author as LLM use. This implies LLMs solve standard counts-format Bayesian problems almost perfectly.
numbers: N=148 in two pilots. 57% of Pilot 2 participants scored 5/5, against a meta-analytic ceiling of about 24% for a single natural-frequency problem.
limits: Abstract only. Indirect: LLM accuracy is inferred from human samples, not measured. Textbook problems are likely in training data, so success says little about novel cases.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 (indirect): on textbook counts problems LLMs are far above human norms, so format may matter less for them. A direct test on novel-number problems is still missing.

source: Cureus (2026) Case mix and protocol constraints in diagnostic LLM conversations: secondary analysis of MedR-Bench outputs
finding: Whether a model keeps asking for tests depends on the case, the simulator and the protocol, not just the model. An apparent link between 'no information available' and reaching the limit shrank to near zero within a case.
numbers: 7 models, 957 reports, 5,719 first-feedback runs. Marker in 80.3% of first feedbacks. Raw difference 6.37 points (95% CI 4.16-8.54); with report and model effects 1.05 (-1.64 to 3.74). 1,001 runs reached the fifth response, all under a forced final-answer prompt. Marker status differed in 23.0% of paired one-round vs free-turn releases for identical case text.
limits: Abstract only. About protocol artefacts in stopping, not the right stop rule.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: measured stopping behaviour is confounded by protocol. Any stop-rule comparison must fix the simulator and turn cap, and report within-case results.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: question-asking LLMs and a benchmark for reliable interactive clinical reasoning
finding: Directly prompting LLMs to ask questions makes diagnosis worse; abstention-style confidence gating that decides when to ask helps.
numbers: Abstract: abstention strategies improve accuracy by 22.3% (base not stated in the abstract). Prompting to ask 'degrades performance' (no magnitude given). Systems still lag an upper bound with full information.
limits: Abstract page only this session. The earlier c19 line gives -11.3% relative; not re-checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (partial): confidence-gated asking beats always-ask, but no comparison of posterior margin vs information-gain floor was found.

source: Brodeur et al. (2026) Performance of a large language model on the reasoning tasks of a physician, Science
finding: Published version of the o1 evaluation: five experiments plus a real emergency-room second-opinion study; the LLM beat physician baselines in all experiments.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract. Europe PMC lists it as citing Rodman 2023.
limits: Abstract only; probabilistic-reasoning details not opened. Same dataset family as Morgan and Rodman, so not independent.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: no recalibration of newer models on the Morgan vignettes was found; this is the newest linked version and predates GPT-5-class models.
